title: Tenor becomes the fashion: Herschel Evans and Ben Webster
summary: Phillips says nobody wanted tenor in the 1920s; later Herschel Evans and Ben Webster took it up, with Webster learning saxophone from Mr. Young after starting on piano.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Because he always told me he was going... He said, 'One of these days I'm going to play just tenor. I like it.' Because the tenor was getting to be a fad; you know, people wanted to hear tenor. But see, when we came along, then, nobody paid no attention to no tenor. All

anybody wanted to hear was alto. Tenor? Who was going to play... Bud Freeman? Didn't nobody listen to him much. You'd hear guys talking about Hawkins. But then, when Les came along, he started playing tenor, there was Herschel...

That's when guys started playing tenors. Ben Webster. Mr. Young taught Ben how to play saxophone. Ben was a piano player. He was playing and violin. Ben said, "I used to hear ole Les in the room, man, playin' that horn, and I'd get in there and try to run over and play, but that cat was gone." But Ben learned fast, you know. He was fooling with alto first, and then he got on tenor, but in a... He stayed with Mr. Young I guess about a year playing piano, and then he was practicing on the saxophone at the same time. In about a year, he came up, man, with Jap Allen's band. They came up all out through the West with Jap Allen's band, and Ben was a sensation. Cats wasn't blowin' tenor like he was blowin' then.
He was kind of into Hawkins, wasn't he?
Yeah. He was on a Hawkins kick. You've heard him play.
Yeah. The Bennie Moten stuff was the earliest I've heard.
You didn't hear him play with Duke?
Oh yeah, I know. But I'm talking about back at that
Yeah, but he was playing with Bennie Moten then.
I've heard him play with Bennie Moten in 1932...
